segments.text: Good day.
This morning, the FOMC decided to maintain the target rate for the federal funds rate
at three and three-quarters to four percent in support of the Federal Reserve's dual mandate.
Economic activity is expanding at a strong pace, while uncertainty remains owing in part
to geopolitical developments.
Domestic spending has been resilient.
Productivity growth is strong, and capital investment robust.
Job gains have kept pace with the workforce, and the unemployment rate has changed little,
but inflation remains elevated.
The Committee believes that the accumulation of more information will help it determine
the policy stance appropriate to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2 percent goal.
the Committee will deliver price stability. At each policy meeting, my
colleagues and I assess the economy by looking out the window. It's what we call
interrogating reality. To gauge what's really going on, it is not a task that
has grown easier. So what exactly do we observe? Economic growth has
strengthened. The GDP increase in the first half of this year was revised
up from an earlier estimate of 1.8 percent up to 2.4 percent and the third
quarter appears to have brought an even more rapid advance led by healthy
consumer spending likely running above 3 percent growth and business
investment likely rising at about a double-digit pace. Capital expenditures
are at a historically high share of GDP. High-tech investment is leading the
acceleration. But there's also been a broadening in other categories and these
trends bear watching. What about the jobless rate? The jobless rate is lower
than a year ago and payroll growth is noticeably above last year's pace. The
four-week moving average of unemployment insurance claims continues to run at
the lowest level in generations. So on the employment side of the Fed's dual
mandate conditions are quite positive and yet Americans of course are still
dealing with inflation that has been running above the committee's objective
for close to six years. It's our responsibility to get inflation down.
That's the reason the FOMC's discussion over the last couple of days focused
mainly on the price stability side of our remit. Since our policy action in
September, we have started to see some changes in financial and credit conditions.
They have tightened for some businesses and households, much as we would expect.
Market participants are becoming somewhat more discerning in their capital allocations,
and while overall financial conditions are tighter, I'm unwilling and unable to call
them tight.
But broadly, these developments go in the direction of achieving a longer, more durable
period of economic growth and price stability.
Over the last couple of days, the committee had a good discussion of the changes in the
economic and financial landscape that marked this inter-meeting period.
We discussed geopolitical developments and fast-moving changes in technology.
We observed, but we're not surprised, that financial markets showed bouts of volatility
in shifting correlations.
So as we widen the frame to survey the broad economic and financial picture, real activity
is clearly pointing in the right direction.
That's good news.
But inflation is too high.
Energy and related prices have moved higher again in recent weeks.
And our job is to ensure that relative price changes in some sectors do not broaden out
across the economy, and that inflation expectations remain as they are anchored.
While these uncertainties are real, there's no lack of clarity in our purpose at the Fed.
Since becoming chairman just five months ago, I've been honored to work with FOMC policymakers
who are unambiguous in their commitment to stable prices.
We've made clear our readiness to act as circumstances require, and we have shown our willingness
to act.
The information we receive over the coming period will help us determine where we want
policy to be.
And at every turn, good or bad, our job is to get monetary policy right.
And that's exactly what we're doing.
Now, with this objective in mind, we've decided on a change in our FOMC schedule starting
next fall.
We believe eight meetings per year is the right number for the FOMC, but in 2027, one meeting
will focus exclusively on broad monetary policy strategy, with neither a vote on the federal
funds rate nor a policy statement anticipated.
The rest will be regular FOMC policy setting meetings, and I expect that in
2028 we'll have two meetings dedicated discussions of strategy and six for
setting policy. Now what's the reasoning behind this change? To me it's quite
straightforward. Getting policy right involves assessing near-term
developments at timely, regular, and information-rich intervals, but it's
Equally important, we reserve time and space
as an intellectually diverse group
for strategic deliberations, for thinking anew
about big questions, looking out over longer time horizons,
focusing, as I say, on the left side of the decimal point.
I believe the setting of the meeting schedule and agenda
is more than some administrative detail.
It's an institutional choice affecting
the nature and the quality of our deliberations
and ultimately, the wisdom of our decisions.
It's yet another change to get the conduct
of monetary policy on the right track.
I appreciate your attention this afternoon.
Now my time is yours and I welcome your questions.
Thank you.
I'm Colby Smith with the New York Times.
There's been essentially no progress
toward the 2% inflation target.
The labor market remains stable,
as you suggested in your opening statement,
and most of your colleagues seem to be on board
with raising rates in December, so why not just raise rates today?
So it's a good question.
I will say I read your stories the last day or two, so I must admit I sort of saw that
question coming.
What I said in my prepared statement was information coming in the coming period will help us tell
us where we want to be, but I suspect you want a little more than that, so let me give
it a shot.
But ensuring price stability, Colby, quashing inflation is not about some fixed individual
date on a calendar.
Same way it's not about some isolated data point.
If it were about those two things, this job would be easier and we wouldn't be suffering
from nearly six years of inflation above target.
So what's this about?
It's about ensuring we have clear objectives, and it's about a monetary policy strategy,
which might sound a year-year in others, like a change from the last several years.
So let me step back.
In the five months or so that I've been around, we've put in place what I describe as new
monetary medicine.
What's been in that package of medicine?
medicine. First thing we did when we showed up with my colleagues is we doubled down on
the 2% inflation target. We said, we own it. We're taking responsibility for it. And if
you think that we're tolerating some inflation target somewhere in the twos, let us disabuse
you of it. That was the first part of this new monetary medicine. Second part is we took
responsibility. No anguish of central banking here, no blaming others. It's a third thing
that we've done. We laid out for you and the world our framework. I did it in
Jackson Hole. It was part of the discussion the last couple days of the
framework that many of my colleagues you to as well. This is how we think about how
monetary policy should work. These are the transmission mechanisms and this is
how we're going to deliver. Then what we do? We interrogate reality. We do that
periodically. That's a very useful thing to do. But we don't just talk, we act.
And so in September, when we last met, we acted.
We removed a dose of accommodation.
So what are the signposts about how this new strategy is going?
Inflation compensation, as measured by swaps prices, many other measures.
Inflation compensation is going in the right way.
Inflation expectations, the world is quite unsettled.
If you'd say absent the Fed, what would have happened to expectations, they might
to go on the wrong way.
They've gone the right way too.
So I feel good about those signposts.
The period right in front of us is information rich.
There is a lot that's happening in the world.
My colleagues and I are keen to take notice of it.
So in this coming period,
what do I think we're going to be able to do?
We're gonna be able to figure out
what's the appropriate protocol
as part of this package
that we started to deliver five months ago
to deliver price stability.
I'm encouraged by the progress we've made
in a short period of time,
but if the crux of your question is,
you haven't delivered yet,
you haven't achieved price stability,
you're right about that,
but we're working on it.
Thank you, Chair Warsh.
So if I could,
this statement says that the accumulation
of more information will help the committee
determine the policy stance appropriate
to ensure a timely return of inflation to the 2% goal.
Does that mean that the current level
the Fed funds rate might already be the right one?
Well, we've got to determine the appropriate protocol.
If you were listening next to me in that room the last couple of days, the overwhelming consensus,
the overwhelming judgment, is that what we've done in this monastery medicine, starting
to work some, but there's no firm conclusions.
If we had a firm conclusion about the conduct of monetary policy, we'd announce it to much
fanfare today.
What we decided to do was to cold these questions, take stock of where we are, evaluate what
we're seeing out the window, ask ourselves whether the period right in front of us is
likely to provide more clarity on the appropriate protocol.
My judgment, the judgment of my overwhelming number of colleagues is that it would.
Mr. Chairman, before-thanks for taking our questions-before the meeting, several members
of the board and the committee went out and told us that we were going to take more time
and that had a profound effect on the outlook for the funds rate. Were you involved in under-in
discussing that message with them? And if you don't mind, I'm sorry, but a protocol
question, what will be the disclosure-public disclosure on the meetings where you're
not going to have a statement? So two questions, I'm sorry.
There are two questions.
Do you not hear the one question rule?
I did, but I thought there was a protocol thing I could do.
That was like a parliamentary procedure question
you were asking.
That didn't count.
I hesitate to indulge the second question.
I fear what it would do, but let me see if I can do it
and not have the slippery slope among us.
Your first question was about my colleagues.
I've got 18 quite independent colleagues.
If you were inside that room the last couple of days,
you would come to believe that to be true.
One way to test the independence of my colleagues is, I don't know if you've heard, Steve, but
I don't submit a dot, I don't plan on submitting a dot, but the 18 of them do, to suggest somehow
that I am some kind of all-knowing person sending messages out.
That's not the committee of the FOMC that I know.
These are serious, sober, responsible people.
We had a serious sober discussion.
So that's the answer to that.
On the parliamentary question, which doesn't count as a question, I'll just say this.
We've made a decision that at that strategy meeting in 27 and the two strategy meetings
in 28, I do not anticipate making any policy decision, putting out a policy statement.
But what might we come out with?
It's not obvious yet.
There's more news to come on that.
The decision on the new format for the meetings is relatively new.
It was a robust discussion over a couple of meetings of how to handle that.
As we get details of that, which are still now, not until next fall, we'll be prepared
to share them with you.
Hi, Nicole.
Good kind of with Barron's.
Thanks for taking my question.
In September, you mentioned that the Fed has a role in sustaining the economic progress
happening in America right now and in the rising opportunities that come with it.
I'm wondering if you can expand on whether you see this as a mandate and how you intend
to fulfill that mandate.
So the mandate was given to us by Congress.
The mandate was deliver stable prices and deliver full employment all in the context
of financial stability.
Now they gave us some other homework to do on supervision and regulation payments, but
I presume you're talking about monetary policy.
So what's the best thing we can do in this environment looking at our window to deliver
on that remit. Ensure stable prices. I mentioned, I think, at a prior press conference, if you
were trying to do the most harmed, the least well off among us, you would let the last six
years of inflation above the Fed's target, usually well above the Fed's target, you'd
let that continue. So that's the most important thing we can do as we look out the window,
and that's what we plan to do. You probably heard me say this. We will deliver price stability.
No ifs, ands, or buts, and that continues to be the case.
Alan or Mila were some before wanted to ask you about the working groups when we can expect
the reports to come up and if there is anything you can preview for us, whether it's on AI
or data or balance sheets.
These five task forces are hard at work.
I have scarcely seen anything that would constitute a final report, but I have done some periodic
check-ins with them.
And I am impressed by the rigor of the intellectual discussions, by the seriousness of the task
that we've given them.
Now some of the questions that I asked to kick off the reports, they want to answer those
and answer a whole range of other questions, which might go to other task forces.
But I'm impressed by what they're doing.
I gave them, like I told you, a year-end deadline.
I think some but not all of the groups will probably hit their deadline and turn their homework in on time
But that just begins the process by which we're going to be consuming which is intellectually serious work
That's a catalyst for us to think anew about productivity and jobs and an inflation framework
And what's the best data to help us do our job how to think about the balance sheet task force?
These are huge intellectual investments that I think are going to bear fruits in the next policy
conjuncture, unlikely to find their way into this policy conjuncture, given the important role as
consumers of these ideas that my colleagues have. But I will have one small announcement. I
previewed this when I was at an IMF meeting, much to the chagrin of some of my colleagues
around here on November 16th. The Productivity and Jobs Task Force will be doing a field
hearing inviting a broad range of people who have strong views. What are the implications
for jobs in the economy near term, medium term, long term? Is this a productivity miracle
that's going to happen or will it happen slowly? I know I, for one, am keenly interested
in refining my own views on that question, but that task force decided that they wanted
to hear from more people as part of their undertaking.
I plan at attending, I might have a few words to say
at the outset of that conference.
I expect the conference will go three, four hours.
It'll be pretty wonky stuff.
I don't know how good the material will be
for the likes of you and your colleagues,
but it's a purpose to do a lot of listening for me
to interrogate the reality in front of me.
What do experts in their fields think about this?
What are the implications for the dual mandate
that I referenced to your colleague.
Is this going to make it harder or easier for us to achieve price stability over the
next several years?
What are the implications for jobs, medium and long term, but near term too?
So we're going to explore those largely in the public realm on November 16th.
I look forward to seeing you there.
Thank you so much.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
James Rosen with Newsmax.
You spoke of interrogating reality.
Since reality is a no-show here today, I'm going to satisfy myself with interrogating
you.
You spoke earlier in your remarks here today about how
your colleagues are serious and sober people who are
committed to price stability.
In an event in the Oval Office on October 7 of this
year, President Trump said, and I quote,
Kevin is great, but Kevin is one vote out of a board
with numerous people that were put on by Obama and
Biden and a couple by me.
So you have a board that would like to see the
country do badly, in my opinion.
Do you agree with those comments?
So James I appreciate the question. I'm not going to be responding to quotes
from public officials. What I can tell you is my experience in five months here.
We just came out of a heck of a family fight. Serious sober discussion. I think
we came to the right policy decision for this moment and I'm honored to be here
and honored to be the chairman of this group. Chairman Warsh, Mariela Isacapura
with Bloomberg News.
So the economy is strong.
Inflation is well above 2%.
You're saying inflation expectations
are going the right way, but surveys
show that households expect inflation
to remain above the Fed's goal, and not just
for the short term.
Using a hike today, I don't know, waiting for more data.
I haven't really heard the clear arguments
as to that decision.
So do you worry that with today's decision,
households may not believe your pledge
to bring down inflation clearly and at sufficient speed and instead will read
this decision of holding rates steady as a sign that the central bank has in fact
a soft inflation target. Yeah so what I can do is tell you there's no soft
inflation target, there's no implicit inflation target, there's a target of
price stability and it's 2% as measured by PCE. It took six years to for
inflation to have the effect on consumers that you reference, but I would say this.
When consumers interrogate reality, they look outside their window, too.
They go to the gas station, too, and they see that prices are up.
I am not going to be the guy who says that oil prices haven't gone up, and when they
fill up their tank, they don't see it.
And so inflation's gone up in expectations in the very near term, because they're doing
what we're doing, interrogating reality.
But if you look out over the horizon, if you look at most but not all measures, what you
see is households, businesses, financial markets, they have the confidence that they should
have that the central bank will deliver price stability.
Thank you, Mr. Chairman.
Edward Lawrence of Fox Business.
So do you see a direct line correlation between oil prices and the inflation we're seeing
in the United States, and if so, how fast could inflation fall or react to falling oil
prices?
So, I don't want to engage in hypotheticals, but I can look out our window and see what's
happened.
There had been a stable correlation between oil prices as they moved up this year, generally,
and interest rates, not the interest rates that we control, but interest rates set in
the market.
that correlation has been quite strong until very recently. We've seen oil
prices continue to move up, largely due to geopolitical events. We've seen crack
spreads between oil and refined products continue to stay elevated. But what's
happened? Interest rates have rolled over to the downside. I'm not a Wall Street
newsletter. I'm just telling you when I look out the window over the last
several months, that is what we've seen. To the extent that oil prices were to
move lower, again probably due to geopolitical events, that's something
that we're gonna have to interrogate. What are the effects on the Fed's dual
mandate? What are the effects on financial market prices and what are we
gonna do about it? But that's a hypothetical and in fact if we look at
financial market prices, futures prices for oil,
they've moved up over the course of the last several weeks
and I can't help but take note of that too.
Thank you, Claire Jones, Financial Times.
Much of the growth that we're seeing in the US economy now
and quite a bit of the inflation too
is coming from the AI boom.
There's quite a lively debate as to whether or not
this is part of the economy that's sensitive
to interest rates in the same way as, say, housing.
I'd love to get your sense of rates need to rise more,
given that so much of the US economy now
is about AI than it otherwise would
if, say, housing was a bigger part of the story.
Thank you.
Thank you, Claire.
So there was a narrative for quite a while,
maybe even in this room over the course of the last several
press conferences.
Well, they're going to raise rates
rates are talking about raising rates, but it's not going to have any effect on AI because
the returns that investors are expecting are so different.
I was skeptical of that view.
Interest rates get in the cracks.
Interest rates affect directly or indirectly almost everything.
And what have we seen?
Since early September, what we've seen inside of the technology complex, outside of the technology
complex, whether you pronounce it AI or SI, Claire, is up to you, what have you seen?
Interest rates have had an effect.
You see market participants that are discriminating between the kinds of investments they want
to make.
You've seen credit spreads for certain assets widen out, gap out.
For others, you've seen some tightening in financial conditions, but not significantly.
So on the thrust of your question of with respect to the new technology and this investment
surge, do interest rates matter?
I believe they do, and I don't believe that they're somehow divorced from the rest of
the economy.
Secondly, I'll just say this.
It is convenient to say that the strength of the economy is all about this new technology
wave.
In fact, if we look at the data, really including data from the last meeting till this, the
CAPEX story is not just robust, not just strong, but it is broadening.
And so if you want to tell the story somehow that this is strength we're seeing only
in narrow pockets, that's a much harder story to tell now than it would have been several
quarters ago.
Thanks so much, Elizabeth Schulze with ABC News.
As you know, the midterm elections are in six days.
Did the midterms factor into the Fed's decision to stay on hold?
And if not, how can you assure the American public that politics were not at play here?
So politics played no role in the decision.
I just spent two days with my colleagues upstairs.
I didn't hear an utterance about politics.
I didn't hear a reference to politics, elections, what's happening in the next week or so.
I didn't hear anything about it.
And I don't believe it had any role in the decision, not just for me, but my colleagues
around the room.
But I will say it's an information-rich interval in the coming period, having nothing to do
with politics.
Hi, thank you, Chris Ruger at Associated Press. I know you don't like the statement
of economic projections, but last month they did, your colleagues penciled in,
another rate hike for this year. And so could you give us your sense from this
meeting, whether you still see widespread support for another hike this year
around the table? Thank you. So the blackout period for them ends I think on
Friday or at some point over the weekend, so they might they might indulge
you in that discussion. I don't believe in forward guidance, absent exigent
circumstances, absent a crisis. I have to give that caveat because in the darkest
days of the 2008 financial crisis, in part using some literature and thinking
from a very recent Nobel Prize winner, that kind of forward guidance is
actually quite helpful. But in normal ordinary times, especially times where
or the underlying real economy is this strong.
I don't believe in it, I don't favor it.
I also don't believe in prejudging meetings.
A lot of things can happen.
So I'm not gonna be able to share with you my musings
about what happens when this group gets together
six weeks from now.
But my judgment is that we might learn a lot
and like in my response to Colby's question,
will be, I think, better positioned to determine the right policy decision and the stance of policy.
Hi, my name is Sang-un Lee from the Korea Economic Development paper. I got a question as a foreign
press. You have spoken several times about the possibility of the Fed shrinking its balance
sheet further. If that plan moves forward later, how would you avoid disrupting foreign
official holders of treasuries or dollar funding markets abroad like South Korea and Japan.
So thank you for your question.
First off, I would say I pay probably more attention to the Korean economy than you might
think because when I'm looking at the feed stocks effectively for this new surge in technology,
a lot of it's coming from Japan and Korea, some from Singapore.
So I'm particularly interested in what's happening in the Korean economy usually because it's telling me what's on planes and ships coming this way.
Secondly, I should say that your new central bank governor is someone I've known for 20 years and is a very talented guy and a good friend, so I'm glad he's in that post.
He and I met actually about 20 years ago amid the global financial crisis as it would come to be known.
And I remember this is a generation of discussions with him about the use of the balance sheet
in exigent circumstances like we had then.
At this point, the balance sheet is solely within the four walls of the balance sheet
task force.
Now, I have checked in with them, full disclosure.
They're working away and comparing their best thoughts.
And I think the conclusions they come to, the recommendations they come to, will be fed
into the FOMC, probably early in the first quarter, but don't hold me exactly to that
timing, and if we decide to make changes in the balance sheet, it will be after a serious
consideration of their proposals and their recommendations.
I think it is unlikely to have any material effect on this policy conjuncture, but it's
a question we should get to the bottom to, and I look forward to doing it with the help
of the outside task force.
Nick Temerosa, The Wall Street Journal. Chairman Warsh, I want to follow up on
your answer to Claire's question. As the AI investment boom becomes more
dependent on external financing, does that make aggregate demand more
sensitive to interest rates than it was before? And related to that, when you
removed a dose of accommodation last month, did you see about what you
bargained for? So you gave me two questions and neither of them were
ahead of any sort of parliamentary out, so you're giving me the opportunity to choose
which of those.
So I'll answer your second question.
When we removed a dose of accommodation, I don't know, six weeks ago, we don't have
perfect foresight on what financial markets are going to do with it, but broadly I would
say the effects on financial markets, on financial market conditions, broadly were consistent
with my expectations.
Howard Stein with Reuters.
Thank you, Chairman.
I'm going to take Nick's first question then.
Give it to me again.
I don't remember.
No.
It's about aggregate demand and the components of inflation.
A lot of your colleagues have said they felt the investment boom in AI was now adding
a strong demand component to inflation.
and this was a handoff from the supply side concerns that might be expected to
fade over time. How much do you think demand is adding to inflation right now
and how sensitive will that be to Fed control? Good, good, good, good, good
pickup of that, good team effort. So I'd say this, the only things we really
they know in economics and supply and demand cross.
Our measures of the size and the shape
of the aggregate demand curve is imperfect.
Broadly what I heard in the room the last couple of days
is consistent with my own views,
which is the economy is strong.
I didn't try to sugar coat that
in the first part of my statement.
The economy has been marked up for the first three quarters.
The economy is pointing in the right direction.
Is the economy running too hot?
Is the economy running too strong?
That isn't the judgment of most of my colleagues.
Part of it is we never know what potential growth really is, Howard.
My judgment is we have seen an improvement in productivity.
We can't measure it precisely.
I think most of that change in productivity precedes everything we're talking about,
about super intelligence, but productivity has been moving higher in the economy, however
imperfectly measured, I think for a couple of years.
And so economic growth is higher, but that doesn't tell me that economic growth is somehow
causing inflation and making our job harder.
But we'll be continuing to look at those issues.
The goal, in my view, and you've heard me say this before, isn't to throw sand in the
gears of the economy and throw people out of work.
I don't think we have to do that.
The dominant means in which this policy is going to be put into practice is we are tightening
financial conditions.
They've tightened a bit since we met last time.
That isn't something that we're uncomfortable with.
That tells me that policy is working, and I think we can do that and make the economy
more durable, have it last longer, and still achieve stable prices.
Hi, Chair Warsh.
Victoria Guido with Politico.
I wanted to ask, next week is a hearing at the White House on Lisa Cook's future and
allegations that have been made against her.
Are you personally or the Fed, as an institution, going to be involved at all in those proceedings?
Not to my knowledge.
Thank you.
Thank you, guys.
